Johann Sebastian Bach. A German Baroque composer and organist born in 1685 and died in 1750 whose mastery of counterpoint and fugal form stands unmatched in Western music history. Working throughout his life in Germany first as a church organist, later as Kapellmeister or court music director at the court of Köthen and in Leipzig, Bach synthesized contrapuntal complexity with harmonic richness and spiritual depth. His vast output of sacred and instrumental works established principles of composition that remain foundational to music theory and practice.

The Art of Fugue, incomplete and published after his death, is his monumental exploration of fugal technique, featuring eighteen fugues and canons of increasing complexity built on a single subject. The Well-Tempered Clavier, in two volumes with twenty-four preludes and fugues each in all major and minor keys, is a pedagogical masterpiece demonstrating the viability of equal temperament tuning and remains essential to keyboard musician training. The Musical Offering is a multi-movement work for various ensembles based on a theme submitted by King Frederick the Great of Prussia, showcasing Bach's ability to transform a simple melody into intricate contrapuntal variations.

As an organist, Bach pioneered the expansion of organ music, composing numerous toccatas, fugues, and works for organ solo, which established the organ as a major concert and compositional instrument. He had at least twenty children, several of whom became important composers in their own right: Wilhelm Friedemann, Carl Philipp Emanuel, Johann Christian, and Johann Christoph Friedrich shaped the Classical period's emergence. He held positions in Weimar, Köthen, and Leipzig, where he served as Thomas Cantor, director of music at the Thomas Church, for nearly twenty-seven years, composing hundreds of sacred cantatas for weekly performance. Bach is the supreme master of counterpoint, and his works are the canonical study texts. The form of the fugue and Bach are nearly synonymous in music education, and he stands as the culminating figure of the Baroque era's harmonic and contrapuntal sophistication.
